client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. I just can't seem to focus at work — I'll be in the middle of something and then my mind just goes blank, or I start thinking about her and lose track of everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because it's not like anything can change what happened.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief is one of the heaviest things we carry, and what you're describing, that sudden blankness and those waves of memory, makes complete sense given what you've been through. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I'd never suggest otherwise; but sometimes talking isn't about changing the past, it's about helping *you* move through it with a little less weight. I'm curious — when your mind drifts to her in those moments at work, what kinds of thoughts or memories tend to surface for you?

client: It's usually the last few weeks before she died — I keep replaying moments where I could have visited but didn't, because I was too caught up with deadlines at work. And then I feel this awful guilt, like I chose spreadsheets over her, which I know sounds terrible but that's genuinely how it feels. It's hard to just let those thoughts pass when they feel so true.
therapist: That doesn't sound terrible at all — it sounds like someone who loved their grandmother deeply and is now measuring that love against an impossible standard in hindsight. What I gently want to invite you to notice is that the thought "I chose spreadsheets over her" is one interpretation of those moments, but there may be other truths sitting alongside it — like that you were doing your best to manage real responsibilities, possibly even ones that supported your life and hers. What do you think your grandmother would have said about the kind of person you were to her, beyond those last few weeks?

client: I know she probably would have said something kind — she always did, she wasn't the type to hold things against people. But that almost makes it worse, because it feels like I'm using her imagined forgiveness to let myself off the hook, and I'm not sure I deserve that yet. It's like the guilt has become this way of proving I actually cared, and if I just... release it, then what does that say about me?
therapist: What you just said is incredibly insightful — you've identified something really important, that the guilt has taken on a *purpose* for you, almost like it's become a tribute to her. But I want to gently ask: is it possible that love and care can be honored in ways that don't require you to keep hurting yourself, and that releasing guilt isn't the same as releasing her? What might it look like to carry her memory in a way that feels meaningful, but doesn't cost you quite so much?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I genuinely don't know what that would look like in practice. Like, are we talking about doing something in her memory, some kind of ritual or gesture? Because that feels a bit abstract to me right now, and I'm worried it would just feel hollow rather than actually helping.
therapist: That's a really honest and grounded response, and it's okay that grand gestures don't feel right — grief doesn't always need a ceremony, sometimes it just needs small, genuine moments of connection to who she was. Rather than thinking about a ritual, I'm wondering if we could start somewhere much simpler — like noticing, in ordinary moments, when you're living out something she valued or taught you, almost like carrying a quiet piece of her forward in how you already move through the world. Can you think of anything about the way you live or the person you are that you can trace back to her influence?

client: She was really big on showing up for people — like, not in a showy way, but just being reliable and present when it mattered. And I think I do try to do that with my friends, though lately I've been pulling away from everyone because I just don't have the energy. I guess I can see the connection, but it also makes me feel worse right now because I feel like I'm failing at the very thing she modeled for me.
therapist: It's worth pausing on something you just revealed — you *did* show up, reliably and consistently, in the way she taught you, and the fact that you're struggling to do that right now isn't failure, it's grief doing what grief does, temporarily dimming the very best parts of us. There's actually something quietly beautiful in the fact that pulling away *bothers* you, because it means that value she gave you is still alive in you, even when you can't fully live it out right now. I'm curious — is there one person in your life, just one, with whom even a small moment of connection this week might feel manageable rather than overwhelming?

client: There's probably my friend Dara — she's checked in on me a couple of times and I've mostly just sent short replies and left it at that. I think I could maybe respond more honestly to her next message, but I'm nervous that if I actually open up, it'll become this whole heavy conversation that I don't have the capacity for right now. I don't want to burden her, and I also don't want to start crying at a bad time and then feel worse than before I reached out.
therapist: It sounds like Dara has already shown you she wants to be there, and what you're describing — the fear of being a burden, of losing control emotionally — are really common thoughts that often protect us from connection but can also quietly reinforce the isolation. I wonder if there's a middle path here, where being more honest with Dara doesn't have to mean opening the whole door at once; even something simple like "I'm struggling more than I've let on, but I'm not ready to talk fully yet — just wanted you to know" is a genuine act of showing up, in exactly the way your grandmother modeled. What feels like the smallest version of honesty you could offer her that would feel true without feeling like too much?

client: I think I could probably tell her something like "I'm having a harder time than I've been letting on" without going into everything, and that actually doesn't feel completely impossible. But I'm second-guessing whether that's fair to her — like, am I just dropping something heavy on her and then leaving her to worry without giving her anything to work with? I guess I'm not sure how to be honest without it feeling like I'm creating a problem for someone else to carry.
therapist: It's really touching that even in the middle of your own pain, you're thinking so carefully about Dara's experience — that's actually you showing up for her, in a quiet way, right now. But I'd gently offer that letting someone who loves you know you're struggling isn't dropping a burden on them; for most caring friends, being trusted with that honesty is a gift, and being kept at arm's length is often harder to sit with than the truth. What do you imagine Dara would actually want — to be protected from knowing, or to be let in just a little?

client: Honestly, if I think about it from her side, Dara would probably want to know — she's the kind of person who would feel hurt later if she found out I'd been struggling and hadn't told her. But knowing that logically and actually sending the message feel like two very different things, and I'm worried that once I do it, I won't be able to control where it goes from there. I think I'm scared of my own emotions more than I am of burdening her, if I'm being honest.
therapist: That last sentence took real courage to say, and I think it's one of the most important things you've shared today — because it shifts the question from "how do I manage Dara?" to "how do I be with myself?" The fear of your own emotions makes complete sense when grief feels this big and unpredictable, but emotions, even the overwhelming ones, do move through us when we let them rather than brace against them. What do you think you're most afraid would happen if you did let yourself feel the full weight of this, even just for a few minutes in a safe moment?

client: I think I'm afraid that if I really let myself feel it, I'll just fall apart completely and not be able to pull myself back together — like there's no bottom to it, and I'll just keep sinking. It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but it genuinely feels like the grief is this enormous thing I've been holding at arm's length because I don't trust myself to survive it fully. And I have to function, I have work and responsibilities, so I can't afford to just collapse.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like someone who has been carrying something enormous largely alone, and has had to stay functional while doing it, which takes an incredible amount of energy. What I want to gently offer is that the fear of "no bottom" is one of grief's most convincing lies; in reality, emotions — even devastating ones — are more like waves than an endless ocean, and people who let themselves feel grief fully almost always find they do come back up, often feeling lighter rather than more broken. I'm wondering, has there ever been a time in your life when you felt something deeply and feared it would overwhelm you permanently, but it didn't — and what got you through that?

client: There was a bad breakup a few years ago where I genuinely thought I wouldn't feel okay again, and eventually I did come through it — but I had friends around me then, and I wasn't trying to hold it together at work the same way. I think the difference now is that I've been so isolated with this that there's no one who really knows how bad it is, so it feels more precarious somehow. I'm not sure the wave metaphor fully lands for me yet, but I can at least acknowledge that I've survived hard things before, even if this feels different.
therapist: You just did something really significant — you found your own evidence that you can survive hard things, and you also identified something genuinely important: that isolation is making this feel more precarious, not the grief itself. That's not a small insight, because it points directly toward something that could actually shift things — and it connects back to Dara, and to the message you were already considering sending. I wonder if what you've just recognized in this conversation might make that message to her feel a little less like a risk and a little more like exactly what got you through the last hard thing?
